Business.title: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial
Business.summary: Predicting a final destination for reset negotiations between the EU and the UK is futile, given the wider challenges that Brussels is facing At the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Emmanuel Macron was pictured apparently waving a grinning Andy Burnham to a seat at the head of the table, as Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, looked on. It was the visual equivalent of the “ welcome back ” message delivered by the French president in the early autumn, following Mr Burnham’s suggestion that rejoining the EU was an option for the UK to consider. At the time, Le Monde was among the media outlets to try out an updated portmanteau to mark the moment; mercifully, “ Breturn ” has yet to catch on. By Friday, the mood music will be louder still. A long-awaited reset summit is due to deliver the first fruits of Mr Burnham’s ongoing rapprochement with Brussels, in the form of new deals on food and drink, and emissions trading. A symbolically powerful youth exchange agreement is also in the works, although not yet over the line. But as they promote such adjustments to existing Brexit arrangements, the prime minister’s allies have been notably keen to avoid pre-empting the broader “conversation” that he desires on relations with the EU. Business.title: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? | Nils Pratley
Business.summary: The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes. This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words. Continue reading...
